headings.title: Introduction to Computer Systems in Healthcare
headings.content: Computers are essential tools in modern healthcare delivery across Nigeria, supporting everything from patient administration to complex clinical decision-making. A computer system functions through the interaction of tangible physical parts and intangible instruction sets. Understanding these foundational pieces allows nurses to navigate electronic hospital environments effectively, troubleshoot minor glitches, and maintain continuous patient care workflows without unexpected technical interruptions.

headings.title: Hardware Components: Input and Output Devices
headings.content:
Hardware refers to the physical machinery of a computer. Input devices allow users to enter data and commands into the system, while output devices display or present processed information.

- **Keyboard and Mouse**: Standard tools used to type patient notes and navigate hospital software.
- **Barcode Scanners**: Optical devices used at the bedside to verify patient wristbands and match medications correctly.
- **Monitors**: Visual displays that present vital signs, laboratory results, and electronic health records.
- **Printers**: Hardware used to generate hard copies of care plans, prescriptions, or discharge summaries.

headings.title: Hardware Components: Central Processing Unit (CPU) and Memory
headings.content:
The central processing unit, often called the CPU, acts as the brain of the computer, executing instructions and processing clinical data. Alongside the CPU, computer memory holds information temporarily or permanently.

- **CPU (Central Processing Unit)**: Interprets and executes commands from clinical software applications.
- **RAM (Random Access Memory)**: Temporary workspace that holds data currently in use, which clears when the computer is turned off.
- **ROM (Read-Only Memory)**: Permanent memory containing basic startup instructions that the computer needs to boot up.

headings.title: Storage Devices and Health Data Management
headings.content: While memory handles active tasks, storage devices retain data over long periods. In healthcare settings, reliable storage ensures that patient records, diagnostic scans, and institutional policies are preserved safely for future reference. Common storage mediums include hard disk drives (HDDs), solid-state drives (SSDs), and external USB flash drives, as well as cloud-based servers hosted off-site. Nurses must follow hospital protocols when storing or backing up sensitive health data to prevent accidental loss or unauthorized access.

headings.title: Software Components: Operating Systems and Clinical Applications
headings.content:
Software consists of the programs and instructions that tell the computer hardware what to do. It is broadly split into system software and application software.

- **Operating System (OS)**: Manages hardware resources and provides a user interface, such as Windows or Linux.
- **Clinical Application Software**: Specialized programs used by nurses to chart vital signs, review medication schedules, and access diagnostic reports.

headings.title: Computer Networks and Electronic Health Record Connectivity
headings.content: Computer networks link individual workstations together, allowing data to flow seamlessly between departments like the laboratory, pharmacy, and nursing station. Local Area Networks (LANs) connect computers within a single facility, while Wide Area Networks (WANs) link multiple branches together. This connectivity powers Electronic Health Record (EHR) systems, ensuring that patient data entered at a triage desk is instantly visible to the attending physician in the ward.

headings.title: Data Security and Ethical Use in Nursing Practice
headings.content: With patient information stored digitally, protecting privacy is a primary professional duty for nurses. Data security involves using passwords, secure login credentials, and encrypted networks to prevent unauthorized access. Ethical use means accessing only the records necessary for direct patient care and maintaining confidentiality at all times. Leaving a computer terminal unlocked with patient data visible is a common breach of professional ethics and hospital policy.
